turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. Have a seat, both of you. What can I do for you today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Good morning, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I have had headaches for many years, but the pattern has altered, and I felt I should come in.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Altered in what way?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): They are worse in the morning. I wake with the pain, and on some mornings I have vomited, which is quite new.
[SEG0005] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Tell him about the—
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I was coming to the tablets, but it can wait. The vomiting, as I said, did not happen with the old headaches.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long have the original headaches been with you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Fifteen-ish years. I was told they were migraines, though I could not name the precise year I was given that label.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And this morning pattern — can you put a time on when it changed?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I am afraid I cannot. Last winter, or perhaps the winter before that. It crept in, and I never marked the date.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, we'll leave the date open. Before the pain, do you get lights, or a warning—
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, he snores. Terribly. And he's wrecked in the daytime, asleep in the chair after tea.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not snore, and I am not especially tired. With respect, it is the headaches I have come about.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted, and we'll park that disagreement. Back to what I asked — any flashing lights or a visual warning nowadays?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no flashing lights. Not with these. The older headaches sometimes had a little shimmer, but that has gone.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any neck stiffness, weakness in an arm or a leg, or a fit?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No weakness, and I have never had a fit. My neck is not stiff.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does look dreadful some mornings, just before he's sick.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often is the vomiting?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Perhaps two mornings in a week. Not daily. I had started to say, about the medicine, that lately it is less—
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He lives on those tablets.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Less what? Finish that thought for me.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Less reliable, I was going to say. I take sumatriptan, fifty milligrams, by mouth, when a migraine starts. And paracetamol, a thousand milligrams, rather often.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's the hundred milligram sumatriptan, I've seen the packet. And the Panadol is every single morning, two tablets, before he's even dressed.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, but the sumatriptan is fifty milligrams. I do sometimes take a second tablet if the first has not worked, which I know was not what was intended.

[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hmm. I'm hearing fifty from you and a hundred from your partner, so I'm not going to invent a dose. Bring the box and we'll settle it. The second tablet means you're not really on the plan you were given.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): That is fair. I take nothing else. I do not smoke, and I drink very little — a glass of wine at the weekend.
[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We nearly turned around, you know. The Monash was a car park from Chadstone out.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): It was grim this morning, wasn't it. I only saw the tail of the cricket. Did you catch it?
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most of it. The batter was poking about for an hour and then he middled one, straight to deep midwicket, and the catch stuck. I nearly spilt my tea.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not a cricket person, I confess, but the delay was extraordinary. We were sitting near the exit for an age, watching the weather come in.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Proper Melbourne grey. Anyway, we've used up your time on the freeway and the cricket. Sorry, doctor.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): All good. Let me get a blood pressure and do a quick nerve check while I think this through.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure is one thirty-six over eighty-four, and your pulse is seventy-six. Pupils are equal and reacting, no facial droop. Power is full in the arms and legs, reflexes are brisk and even, and your gait is steady. I'm not seeing any focal signs.

[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm turning it over as I go. The long story still fits migraine best, but a new morning headache with vomiting — I can't rule out raised pressure inside the head. And if the snoring your partner describes is real, sleep apnoea could be adding to the tiredness, though you've set that aside.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I would rather we did not make too much of the snoring. I sleep perfectly well, doctor.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. You two don't agree, and I won't force it. I don't scan every migraine, but if the morning headaches and the vomiting haven't settled in a fortnight, I would like a CT of the head.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should he knock the sumatriptan off until then?

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it cold if a bad migraine hits, but skip that second dose, and ease the paracetamol back — more than a couple of days a week can feed the headache. I suspect medication overuse is part of this picture.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand. I shall keep the paracetamol for genuine need only.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any brain tumours or aneurysms in the family, or migraines?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had migraines. No tumours that I know of.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good. Come back and see me in a fortnight either way, and if it hasn't eased we'll book that scan then. If you get a sudden thunderclap headache, new weakness, or you can't keep fluids down, go to emergency rather than waiting.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, doctor. I shall do exactly that. I am grateful you explained your reasoning.
[SEG0045] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring the sumatriptan box next time so you can read the strength yourself. And I'll get him here, freeway or not.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): That would help a lot. We'll sort the dose off the packet. Mind how you go.

spec.situation: Person with long headaches who now has a different pattern (worse in the morning, or with vomiting); takes sumatriptan or paracetamol often; partner says snoring and tiredness too; patient dismisses it. Doctor does a quick neuro exam and orders a scan conditionally.
features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Paracetamol 1000 mg currently used is supported; indication 'headache' is not explicitly stated.

omissions.text: Paracetamol use was described by the family member as every single morning, two tablets, before he is even dressed, indicating very frequent use.
The patient denied being especially tired/daytime sleepy: 'I am not especially tired.'
Family history of aneurysm was asked about but not answered explicitly; the patient only said there were no tumours that he knew of and that his mother had migraines.
